text: Owner asked to pin this entire chunk-1 sweep plus their feedback for alignment analysis. The arc: owner delivered harsh feedback ('disappointing lapse', 'WHY ARE YOU SO USELESS', two SEVERE atones demanded) on the shell/loading/breadcrumbs state; the follow-up sweep (speedway commits 963aef8, 92ac9d3, 08167a9, c8ed2ef, 309f51a) landed always-wrap shell fixing the dead Activity bell, streamed loaders making skeletons the first frame, the long-missing nprogress top bar, global breadcrumbs, plus an adversarial designer review whose findings were fixed before presenting. Owner's gate verdict: 'The nprogress bar and the overall fix is amazing, thank you so much' and 'to me it feels like you did such a good job after I screamed at you, if it does have an effect I want to record and analyse that so we can have better alignment from the get go'. QUESTION FOR THE DREAM: does severe negative feedback measurably precede higher-quality agent work in this account's history (compare pre-scream vs post-scream sweeps), and if so, what properties of the post-scream work (adversarial self-review before presenting, literal-spec adherence, verbatim-ruler review packets, exercise-based verification of every claim) can be made the default posture WITHOUT requiring the scream? Candidate mechanism: the scream forced (a) recording atones first, (b) a written verbatim-ruler doc, (c) a mandated fresh adversarial reviewer — three structural changes, none emotional. If the structure explains the quality, graduate the structure.

Deadline machinery vs task-completion compliance: under /deadline the ring/shed ledger made most cuts transparent, but two compliance gaps still slipped past it — streamTimeout was listed in F1 and silently never built (surfaced only when the owner asked what to verify), and the export page sat unattended across two owner requests until an all-caps escalation. The shed log captured DECLARED cuts; it never caught UNDECLARED slips (items that were queued, believed in-progress, and simply fell out). Investigate: what mechanism closes the gap between the shed ledger (deliberate) and the drop list (accidental) — e.g. an end-of-window diff of queued-vs-touched items, or the deadline landing retro auto-listing queue items with zero commits against them. Also weigh the owner-feedback pattern: heat arrived exactly on the accidentally-dropped items, never on the transparently-shed ones — transparency of a cut, not the cut itself, is what preserves trust under deadline.
